lines.text: Your screen works with a finger, but not with a glove or a pen cap. Why does it only feel you?
Under the glass is an invisible grid of see-through wires. Rows one way, columns the other.
Every crossing point holds a tiny bit of electric charge, like a little bucket. The phone checks every bucket, over and over, more than a hundred times a second.
Your body conducts electricity. So when your finger comes close, it pulls a little charge away from the crossings right under it.
The phone sees which buckets dropped, and works out exactly where you touched, even between the wires.
Two fingers? Each one makes its own dip. That's how pinch-to-zoom knows both spots at once.
A glove or a plastic pen doesn't conduct, so the buckets don't change. To the screen, you're not there.
And water does conduct. That's why raindrops can make your screen go a little crazy.
One touch, and your team is in sync. In Orbi Work, drag a file onto a task, tap a step, and everyone sees it change, live.
orbitransfer.com, slash work. Now you know!
